vignette:
Margaret

Margaret sits in the leather armchair with her hands folded in her lap, her posture precise and controlled—the same posture she's maintained for fifty years in server rooms and network operations centers. At seventy-two, she's been retired for two years, though she still receives calls from her former employer asking her to troubleshoot critical infrastructure problems. She always says yes. The work keeps her mind occupied in ways that retirement hasn't managed to fill.

Three years ago, Margaret was consulting on-site at a financial services firm downtown. She'd gone to the server room on the third floor to install redundancy protocols—work she could do in her sleep after decades in the field. The building was mostly empty; it was a Saturday morning. She was focused on her laptop when she heard the commotion from the hallway. A man had brought a gun into the office. She didn't see him directly, but she heard the shots. She heard them clearly. She also heard her colleague, David, who worked in the cubicles nearby. She heard him cry out, heard the terrible finality of what followed.

Margaret had locked herself in the server room. She sat on the cold floor between two massive cooling units for nearly four hours while police swept the building. She was physically unharmed. David was not.

Since that day, Margaret's relationship with her carefully ordered world has fractured in ways that don't make logical sense to her—and that troubles her deeply. She prides herself on logic, on systematic thinking, on identifying problems and implementing solutions. But the mind, she's discovering, doesn't follow the clean architecture of a well-designed network.

The sounds come without warning. A car backfiring on the street outside her suburban home sends her heart into her throat, and suddenly she's back on that floor, the fluorescent lights buzzing overhead. She's taken to driving only on quiet residential roads, avoiding highways where trucks make sharp noises. Her husband, Richard, has gently suggested she might not need to go out quite so often. She knows what he's really saying: that her fear has become their shared burden.

She's stopped going into the office, even when they call. She tells them it's her age, her health, but the truth is more complicated. The thought of being in that building—any office building—makes her chest tight. She imagines scenarios: exits blocked, no place to hide, the terrible helplessness of being trapped. Her mind, so good at solving technical problems, has become expert at generating catastrophes.

At night, she lies beside Richard, acutely aware of every sound in the house. Sometimes she gets up and checks the locks, though she checked them an hour before. She knows it's irrational. She checks them anyway. Sleep comes in fragments, interrupted by dreams she can't quite remember but that leave her gasping.

What troubles Margaret most is the guilt. She survived. She was in the right place at the right moment. David, who had a daughter in college and a wife who still calls their house sometimes, didn't have that luck. Margaret feels the weight of that randomness, that arbitrary mercy. She wonders sometimes if she should have done something different, though she knows—logically knows—that there was nothing she could have done.

Richard brings her coffee each morning. She sits by the window and watches the neighborhood wake up. She's thinking about calling someone, a therapist perhaps, though the idea of talking about it feels like admitting that the trauma has won, that she can't simply process and move forward like she does with every other problem in her life.
